https://nineoclock.ro/turkiye-takes-part.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Constanța, 15 August 2026 – Türkiye, Romania’s NATO Ally and strategic partner in the Black Sea, will take part on Saturday, 15 August, in the events marking the 124th anniversary of Romanian Navy Day with the Turkish Navy’s TCG KEMALREİS (F-247) frigate and TCG BURGAZADA (F-513) corvette, as well as the Turkish Coast Guard Command’s TCSG DOST vessel. The participation comes just five weeks after the delivery to the Romanian Naval Forces of the corvette “Rear Admiral August Roman,” the first large new combat ship to join the Romanian Navy in over 30 years. During their stay in Constanța, the three vessels are open to the Romanian public during designated visiting hours, and naval personnel and defence industry representatives from both countries are meeting in Constanța. “The presence of our Navy and Coast Guard vessels at Romanian Navy Day reflects a solid, long-standing defence partnership with Romania. Just weeks after the delivery of the ‘Rear Admiral August Roman,’ we reaffirm Türkiye’s commitment to remaining a trusted naval partner for our Black Sea ally,” said Musa Heybet, Deputy Minister of National Defence of the Republic of Türkiye and Chairman of the Board of Directors of ASFAT. A Bilateral Relationship Spanning Nearly a Century The solidarity between Türkiye and Romania is not a recent development, but the continuation of a bilateral relationship built over nearly a century. In a speech delivered at Ankara Palas on 17 March 1937, in honour of Romanian Foreign Minister Victor G. Antonescu, the founder of the Republic of Türkiye, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, said: “Nations are bound more by sentiment than by treaties. Romania holds a fraternal place in our hearts.” Türkiye’s participation in Romanian Navy Day with three vessels, shortly after the delivery of the “Rear Admiral August Roman,” confirms the continuity of this relationship in a practical format, oriented toward concrete defence industry cooperation. “Rear Admiral August Roman” Corvette: A Commitment Kept The “ Rear Admiral August Roman ” (261) corvette, of the HISAR class, was sold to Romania under an intergovernmental agreement signed in December 2025, Built by ASFAT at Istanbul Naval Shipyard Command, the vessel was handed over to the Romanian Naval Forces at a ceremony held in Istanbul on 20 June 2026, in the presence of Presidents Nicușor Dan and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan , and arrived in Constanța on 10 July 2026. The delivery, completed within six months of the contract’s signing, also marks Türkiye’s first export of a military vessel to a country that is a member of both NATO and the European Union. With a length of approximately 99.5 metres and a displacement of around 2,300 tonnes, at a top speed of over 24 knots, “ Rear Admiral August Roman ” is equipped with a 76mm main gun, remotely operated weapon stations, a fire-control radar with an integrated electro-optical sensor, electronic warfare systems, a hull-mounted sonar and an integrated, NATO-interoperable communications suite. The vessel is intended for surveillance, reconnaissance, patrol, maritime interdiction and search-and-rescue missions, as well as surface, anti-air and anti-submarine combat operations, including the operation of an embarked helicopter. “The delivery of the ‘Rear Admiral August Roman’ within six months of signing the intergovernmental agreement confirms ASFAT’s ability to manage complex naval programmes on schedule. The participation of Turkish vessels in Romanian Navy Day is a natural continuation of this partnership and evidence of our readiness for new joint projects,” said Prof. Dr. Mustafa İlbaş , CEO of ASFAT. Delivery Timelines: A Strategic Factor in Naval Modernisation In today’s security environment, the ability to deliver naval platforms on schedule has become as important a criterion as technical performance. Amid rapidly evolving regional risks, countries that either have ready platforms or can produce them quickly gain a strategic advantage. ASFAT points to the delivery of the “Rear Admiral August Roman” — completed within six months of the contract’s signing — as an example of the Turkish industry’s ability to manage complex naval procurement programmes while meeting agreed timelines. ASFAT’s Program Director and Country Manager for Romania will also take part in the events in Constanța, in discussions with Romanian authorities and industry representatives on the future equipment requirements of the Romanian Naval Forces. Outlook for Broader Cooperation Military and defence cooperation between Türkiye and Romania could be expanded in the period ahead through: a potential second corvette project similar to the “Rear Admiral August Roman” project; local production and industrial cooperation, particularly through new-build programmes and technology transfertechnology transfer and local production. shipyard operations and management; unmanned naval platforms; modernisation, maintenance and repair services; logistics support and lifecycle services; About ASFAT ASFAT (Askeri Fabrika ve Tersane İşletme A.Ş.) is a wholly state-owned company under the authority of the Ministry of National Defence of the Republic of Türkiye. The company operates military shipyards and defence factories and acts as the prime contractor for Türkiye’s naval programmes, including exports carried out through intergovernmental agreements. ASFAT representatives note that the nearly century-long friendship between Türkiye and Romania, reinforced through the “Rear Admiral August Roman” project, provides a solid foundation for deepening bilateral naval cooperation. https://www.dw.com/en/japan-s-empty-temp.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5M8bM Centuries-old temples like Odawara are struggling to stay relevant in modern Japan Image: Alexander Pöschel/imageBROKER/picture alliance Advertisement The 370-year-old structure has all the attributes of a classically designed Japanese temple , from the curved roof to the timber-frame walls, spacious tatami-mat prayer hall and elaborately decorated altar. Set in manicured gardens on the Chita Peninsula in central Japan , the 350-square-meter (3,767-square-foot) property is on the market for 482 million yen (€2.66 million, US3.01 million). The estate agent's pitch says the price includes dismantling by "expert heritage craftsmen" and delivery to anywhere in Japan, where it would be fully restored into a "stunning" two- or three-bedroom home. The sale and removal of the temple marks the end of its role in the local community in the hills above the Nagasawacho district, but it is a better fate than many places of worship across Japan. There are around 77,000 temples across the country, but as many as 17,000 no longer have a full-time resident priest as congregations have shrunk — particularly in rural districts experiencing rapid depopulation — and financial pressures have taken their toll. That means many temples are being sold off or simply shuttered and left to deteriorate quietly. A temple brought back to life Tomomi Iwayama took on the abandoned Ganshu-ji temple in Odawara, a coastal town about 80 kilometers (50 miles) southwest of Tokyo, a decade ago. Today, he is the abbot of a growing congregation. "The temple had no abbot for 70 years before I arrived because it was just so difficult to operate, and it has taken me until now to get it financially back on track," he told DW. "Even in a relatively large urban area such as Odawara, which has around 200,000 residents, it has been very hard," he said. "In the countryside, it is much more difficult." Iwayama's biggest problem is the country's shrinking population : fewer worshippers and falling demand for funerals and other traditional rites make it harder to finance the temple's upkeep. He has worked hard to reach out to the local community and has had success in selling plots in the temple graveyard. Odawara Castle was built in the mid-15th century Image: Koji Sasahara/AP Photo/picture alliance One innovation that has attracted attention is the temple's "smart graveyard," where families scan a card, and a robotic system recovers a relative's ashes from the columbarium. Temples in rural areas of Japan face far greater challenges, he said. "Young people in villages usually leave to go to university, and then they find a job in one of the big cities, so they rarely go back," he said. "Maybe they will go back once a year to pay their respects to their ancestors at the village temple, but that is not enough for the temple to get by on." Equally, when the head priest of a rural temple retires, his children are unlikely to want to take the role on because of these challenges. All too often, Iwayama said, the result is the temple closing. But he denies the suggestion that religion in Japan is following the same path as in the West, where Christian congregation numbers have plummeted over the decades. Faith in the Digital Age To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Demand for Buddhism remains "I sense there is still a lot of demand in Japan for Buddhism," he said, contrasting the fast-paced, technology-focused lives that people typically lead with the serenity that they are often seeking. "Buddhism is a style of living, of an enlightened person," he said. "A lot of people are looking for that. And while the traditional rituals of funerals and anniversaries are declining and that revenue is shrinking, we are finding that more people want to take part in traditional temple cuisine cooking classes, meditation and other things that we can offer." Temples that are not able to shift to offer experiences more in tune with modern Japan are at risk of closing, said Joey Stockermans, one of the founders of the Mokomoko online real estate service. "We have had a temple on our site in the past, and we were approached by a foreign potential buyer, so there is certainly interest when these properties become available," he said. Other foreigners who are long-term residents are doing their best to protect Japan's religious heritage for future generations. American journalist and author Jake Adelstein is currently a Zen priest at Zenshoin Temple in Tokyo's Toshima Ward and is training to become an abbot. "I do not think that Japanese are becoming less religious; I believe they are becoming fewer because of population decline, and they are becoming less wealthy because of the economic situation," he said. Meet Japan’s AI Buddhist Robot To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "Families want to keep the grave plot that they have had for generations, but for many of them it is just too expensive to maintain, and they often live a long way away, so they are unable to regularly visit to pay their respects," he said. The annual fee for a grave can be up to 100,000 yen, while memorials and other rites can be an additional financial burden, Adelstein explained. Young people shun religious careers "Young people are not interested in a career as a priest because temples earn so little money, so there are positions that cannot be filled, and that is especially a problem in the countryside," he said. Some temples have amalgamated their operations and share a priest, but that will become more difficult in the future, Adelstein said. As elsewhere, Zenshoin Temple has started vegetarian cooking classes and Zen meditation sessions to appeal to the local community, and Adelstein hopes that will be enough to keep the temple open. "The training to become an abbot is very tough, and the economics of a temple today often just do not add up, but I see it as a critical part of this society and this nation," he said. (Ukrainian Ukrzaliznytsia Railway Company Press Office via AP) (Uncredited, Ukrainian Ukrzaliznytsia Railway Company Press Office) WARSAW – Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned on Thursday that Russia is planning hybrid strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, among them Poland. Russia will pretend the attacks are “accidental” in order to “paralyze or at least weaken the motivation of NATO countries" to rush to the defense of the member state coming under attack, Tusk said in a speech to the Polish parliament. Recommended Videos “There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles will enter the territory of one or several countries on the eastern flank and even cause destruction," Tusk warned. “The official narration will be that it’s an accident and there is no reason for NATO to think about a response,” he added. He said Russia was more dangerous because it was increasingly using jet-powered drones, which fly higher and faster and thus are more difficult to detect by air defense before reaching their targets. Tusk has been for months warning that Russia might be preparing a more serious hybrid attack against a NATO country. His warnings have gotten increasingly specific as he received intelligence from NATO, Ukrainian and U.S. secret services, including the CIA, he said. In recent days, Tusk has said Russia was now focusing on attacking border crossings between Ukraine and its European neighbors in order to disrupt delivery lines to Ukraine. Four such incidents happened on Poland's border with Ukraine in the past week and several others took place in the last weeks on Ukraine's border with Moldova. Tusk said at the moment Russia was not ready for any peace talks “without the total capitulation of Ukraine.” “They are convinced the winter will be tragically critical for Ukraine,” Tusk said. He said last winter Poland stepped in with deliveries when Ukraine's energy infrastructure came under attack, but if border crossings are destroyed, it will be much harder for Warsaw to offer such help this upcoming winter. “Russia's goal is to destroy as much as possible the economy and logistics of Ukraine,” Tusk said, adding that intelligence indicates continuous attacks of “very high frequency and intensity” on six main Ukrainian cities should be expected in the near future. Tusk announced on Thursday he would travel to Ukraine overnight to Friday, in what can be seen as an act of defiance against Russia after European leaders narrowly escaped a drone strike on a train near the Polish-Ukrainian border on Sunday. Officials usually keep their travel plans to Ukraine secret for security reasons. In Kyiv, he said he would discuss with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy how to defend against the new types of drones as well as discuss with partners including Slovakia about further sanctions against Russia. On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that “major progress is being made toward establishing a U.S. Army base in Poland” after a U.S. delegation was in Poland last week to visit several possible locations. “If this happens, the location will be announced very soon,” Trump wrote. “This will be a historic step for our Great U.S./Polish Alliance.” Poland has for years sought to host a permanent U.S. base as a strong guarantee of its security in the face of the rising Russian threat. Poland’s high defense spending and major U.S. arms purchases have persuaded the Trump administration to consider putting a permanent base in Poland even as it reorganizes and reduces its overall military presence in Europe. In May, the U.S. unexpectedly withdrew troops from the total of around 10,000 stationed in Poland, causing confusion among European allies and nervousness in Warsaw. But officials in both Poland and the U.S. soon said the withdrawal was temporary and Poland was not expected to suffer from the U.S. troop reorganization. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: BERLIN — Friedrich Merz has tried to move on from his conservatives’ historic defeats to the far right in eastern Germany, but his biggest test as chancellor — and of his grip over his own party — may still lie ahead. The Alternative for Germany is pushing to deliver its biggest blow yet to the chancellor’s weakened coalition government by installing the country’s first far-right state premier since World War II in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt when lawmakers vote on the post in December. Merz’s fellow Christian Democrats in Berlin fear regional members of their own party will help the AfD do this, creating a nightmare scenario for the chancellor. That concern stems from accusations that a group of Saxony-Anhalt conservatives already broke ranks by voting in a secret ballot for the AfD’s candidate for state speaker earlier this month, outraging national conservative leaders. Advertisement Advertisement “The behavior of the CDU parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt with regard to past and upcoming elections is completely unacceptable,” Thomas Röwekamp, a CDU lawmaker who chairs the Bundestag’s defense committee, said. The AfD “wants to annihilate the CDU in Germany” by “forcing us into a debate about how to deal with it in order to divide the party,” he added. “We must not allow that to happen.” Under pressure from conservatives in Berlin, Saxony-Anhalt CDU leader Sven Schulze announced a plan last week to have his party’s lawmakers leave the chamber during the initial two rounds of secret voting in December, ensuring none can vote for the far-right candidate — or be suspected of doing so. It’s unclear what the party would do in a potential third round, when the AfD would only need a majority of votes cast. AfD leaders have openly said they are seeking defections from conservative ranks, a strategy designed as much to sow division among conservatives as to win the premiership. That approach seems to be working, at least partly. Sven Schulze, outgoing Premier of Saxony-Anhalt and member of the German Christian Democratic Union, attends the first session of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament since state elections on October 6, 2026 in Magdeburg. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images State conservatives have faced intense criticism for appearing so divided and vulnerable to aiding the AfD that their leaders apparently have no choice but to avoid the vote altogether. “It’s about taking a stand and assuming responsibility, rather than shirking a decision,” Röwekamp said. Local CDU lawmakers, however, say their approach is tactically necessary. “We have always drawn a clear line between ourselves and the AfD,” CDU state lawmaker Chris Schulenburg said. “We adhere to the principle of distinguishing ourselves on the basis of substance, but not excluding them [the AfD], because, after all, the party is not currently banned, and its parliamentarians were also democratically elected.” AfD leaders, meanwhile, have rejoiced in the CDU’s disarray. Advertisement Advertisement “This is nothing less than the CDU’s capitulation,” AfD national co-leader Tino Chrupalla said after the state conservatives announced their plan to leave the chamber. “They’re afraid of elections.” Centrists flirting with radical s For Merz, whose approval ratings are at historic lows, his party’s conduct in Saxony-Anhalt — and the prospect of a politically explosive AfD victory in December — are complicating efforts to move past last month’s humiliating election losses in eastern Germany and project renewed control as he attempts to focus on core priorities: backing Ukraine and reviving the economy. Already, center-left lawmakers have attacked parts of Merz’s party as having failed to learn the lessons of Germany’s history, drawing parallels with the Nazis’ rise to power with conservative help. The co-leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party Alice Weidel delivers a statement on October 6, 2026 at the Bundestag in Berlin. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images After local conservative lawmakers appeared to back the AfD’s candidate for the Saxony-Anhalt speaker earlier this month, Social Democratic Party (SPD) lawmakers in Berlin marched in protest past the Brandenburg Gate to a square where the Nazis carried out book burnings. SPD Defense Minister Boris Pistorius sang the national anthem and called the episode the breaking of a taboo that “we haven’t seen in this form for more than 90 years.” Conservative lawmakers have retorted in recent weeks by attacking the SPD and Greens for letting their Berlin branches enter coalition talks with the Left — a far-left party rooted in the East German communist party— which won first in the city in last month’s election. But for Merz and his coalition government, the stakes of the December vote in Saxony-Anhalt are far greater. Advertisement Advertisement How the December vote will unfold remains highly unpredictable. Ultimately, the AfD’s candidate for the premiership, Ulrich Siegmund, could win the post with support from Alliance Sahra Wagenknecht, a small, populist-left party that has expressed openness to working with the AfD and shares its Kremlin-friendly views . Merz is clearly alarmed by the prospect of CDU lawmakers covertly assisting the AfD — an outcome that could trigger his chancellorship’s greatest political crisis yet. “People who do things like that — members of parliament who extend a hand — there is no place in the CDU for such a choice, and that will not change,” Merz said earlier this month. “The CDU will never elect extremists to public office or government positions anywhere in Germany.”

https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/12/who-.text: Loading the video Tech News Video. Who is Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy linked to Nvidia's Jensen Huang? Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 12 November 2026 - 15:52 GMT+1 Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese businesswoman who has been at the centre of allegations involving a suspected Chinese intelligence operation targeting Nvidia and its former CEO, Jensen Huang. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT US intelligence agencies believed she had been recruited by Beijing to gather information on one of the world's most valuable technology companies. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang share a surname but are not related. She previously held a senior position at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data centre company that rents computing power to businesses developing and running AI systems. Megaspeed described itself as a key business partner of Nvidia's cloud computing operations in the Asia-Pacific region. Photographs from a technology industry event in 2024 showed the two sitting together. In May 2025, they also attended a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang in Taipei during the Computex technology expo. Video footage from the restaurant showed Jensen Huang putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kissed him on the cheek. They were later seen leaving in the same car. Jensen Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family and colleagues. Nvidia's board subsequently launched an independent investigation into the matter. On Thursday, November 12, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO and board member after 33 years leading the company. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO. Separately, Singapore's authorities confirmed that Alice Huang had been investigated over possible offences involving the purchase and export of servers through Singapore. She left the country in February and was subsequently barred from re-entering. Authorities said the investigation was not related to espionage and that there was insufficient evidence to establish that she had committed an offence. She was issued a stern warning over information provided to investigators.
